title: MINURSO ends: Western Sahara loses its UN monitors
deck: After 35 years, the UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has ended without renewal, leaving a frozen conflict between Morocco and the Algeria-backed Polisario with no neutral observers on the ground.

fuel.title: No UN monitors left on the ceasefire line
fuel.how: With MINURSO gone, nobody neutral watches the 1991 ceasefire line, and the UN itself warns of security risks.

fuel.title: Security Council fails to renew the mandate
fuel.how: The mission ended because the Council did not renew it; Morocco welcomed this, while Polisario and its backers appear to oppose it.

fuel.title: Migration route towards Spain may come under pressure
fuel.how: Greater tension in the region could push more people towards Spain, though the material gives no figures and the link is an estimate.

card.headline: The UN's Western Sahara mission is over, and no one is left to watch the ceasefire

keyNumber.label: MINURSO served in Western Sahara before the Security Council failed to renew its mandate on 1 November 2026

forYou.line: The 1991 ceasefire now has no neutral monitor. Watch the Morocco-Polisario line and Algeria's wider posture.
Moroccan and Algerian ports and routes are not directly hit so far. Treat any clashes near the territory as a risk to watch, not a certainty.
Tension between Morocco, Algeria and the Polisario could affect migration towards Spain. The size of any effect is uncertain.
The UN says it stands ready to keep backing a political solution. The mission is gone, but the dispute is not.

effects.text: MINURSO winds down after the Security Council fails to renew its mandate; no UN monitors remain
Morocco, which claims the territory, welcomes the decision; the Algeria-backed Polisario appears to oppose it
UN Secretary-General Guterres says the UN remains committed to a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for self-determination
The UN warns of security risks now that its observers are leaving
With no neutral reporting, claims and counter-claims about incidents along the ceasefire line become harder to check
Morocco, Algeria and the Polisario each reassess their positions with fewer outside constraints
Sahrawi refugees and civilians in and near the territory lose a UN presence; the humanitarian effect is unclear
Any renewed fighting could pull Algeria and Morocco closer to direct confrontation, as their relations were already strained
Algeria's firmer regional posture, including its troop deployment to Niger, adds to the sense of a shifting Maghreb and Sahel balance
More tension in the region could raise migration pressure towards Spain and test Spain's ties with Morocco

whatHappened: The UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, ended on Sunday 1 November 2026. It had been in place since the 1991 ceasefire, so it lasted 35 years. France 24 reports it ended after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate.

Morocco, which claims the region as its own, welcomed the decision. Its opponents in the Algeria-backed Polisario Front appear to have reacted differently, but our source text on their response is cut off, so we do not describe it in detail.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the UN remains committed to a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. UN News reports the mission began to wind down on the same day. The UN also warned of security risks.
whyItMatters: Security: MINURSO was the only neutral eye on the ceasefire line. Its main job was monitoring the 1991 truce. With observers gone, incidents will be harder to verify, and each side can tell its own story. The UN itself has warned of security risks. Our estimate is that this raises the chance of miscalculation, but the material does not show any fighting yet.

Politics: The mission did not end through a peace deal. It ended because the Security Council did not renew it. That shows how little agreement there is among major powers on how to resolve the dispute. Morocco gains from the outcome. The Polisario and Algeria appear to lose a channel for international attention. The UN says it will still support political efforts, but it now has less leverage on the ground.

Displacement: Western Sahara sits on migration routes towards Spain and the Canary Islands. The summary of this event flags possible knock-on effects for migration towards Spain if tension rises. This is a risk, not an observed trend. We have no figures yet, and the effect depends on whether security actually worsens.

The wider backdrop matters too. Algeria's president has ordered troops into Niger, the first Algerian deployment abroad since 1973. Neither event caused the other, but both point to a more assertive Algerian posture just as UN monitoring recedes.

winners.why: It claims the region and welcomed the end of the mission. It also faces less international scrutiny on the ground.

losers.who: The Polisario Front and Sahrawi advocates
losers.why: They lose the UN's on-the-ground presence, which was tied to the long-promised idea of self-determination.

losers.who: Civilians in and near the territory
losers.why: There are fewer neutral observers and fewer UN eyes if tension rises. The humanitarian effect is unclear.
After 35 years, the mission ended without a settlement and without Council agreement to continue.
It is exposed to any rise in migration and to strained relations if Morocco and Algeria clash. The scale is uncertain.

whatsNext: Watch for reports of incidents near the ceasefire line, and how Morocco and the Polisario describe them.
Watch what role, if any, the UN keeps through the Secretary-General or an envoy. Guterres says the UN stands ready to support peace efforts.
Watch Algeria's posture, including its Niger deployment, and any change in Morocco-Algeria tone.
Watch migration figures at Spain's southern borders and Atlantic routes for early signs of change.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what do you think is the most likely path over the next six months?
options: Quiet drift: the dispute stays frozen, with more rhetoric but little fighting
Low-level clashes along the ceasefire line, with competing accounts
A diplomatic reset that revives talks
Wider escalation involving Algeria and Morocco
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 45%, is quiet drift. Frozen conflicts often stay frozen. But the lack of monitors makes clashes with competing accounts a serious second path, at about 30%. These probabilities are our judgement, not a sourced forecast.

timeline.title: Morocco's Green March into the territory
timeline.detail: As Spain prepared to leave its colony, Morocco moved to take control. Mauritania also moved in, and the Polisario Front began an armed struggle. Background from general knowledge.

timeline.title: Polisario proclaims the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic
timeline.detail: The Polisario, backed by Algeria, declared a state in exile; refugee camps developed near Tindouf in Algeria. Background from general knowledge.

timeline.title: Security Council creates MINURSO
timeline.detail: The mission was set up to monitor a ceasefire and support a referendum on the territory's future. Background from general knowledge.

timeline.title: Ceasefire takes effect
timeline.detail: Fighting between Morocco and the Polisario stopped. The promised referendum was never held.

timeline.title: Ceasefire breaks down
timeline.detail: After an incident at Guerguerat, the Polisario declared the truce over and low-level fighting resumed. Background from general knowledge; details of how the conflict evolved since then are not covered in our sources.

timeline.title: United States recognises Moroccan sovereignty
timeline.detail: A major shift in international positioning that strengthened Morocco's hand. Background from general knowledge.

timeline.title: Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with Morocco
timeline.detail: Relations between the two neighbours worsened sharply. Background from general knowledge.

timeline.title: Spain backs Morocco's autonomy plan
timeline.detail: Madrid shifted its long-held position, a notable change for the Western Sahara file. Background from general knowledge; Spain is a key country for migration links.

timeline.title: MINURSO ends after 35 years
timeline.detail: The Security Council failed to renew the mandate. Morocco welcomed it. The UN warned of security risks and said it stands ready to keep supporting peace efforts.

causes.name: Unresolved sovereignty
causes.detail: Morocco claims the territory. The Polisario, backed by Algeria, seeks self-determination. The two have never agreed on terms.

causes.name: Referendum never held
causes.detail: MINURSO was created to support a vote on the territory's future. In 35 years that vote did not happen.

causes.name: Regional rivalry
causes.detail: Morocco and Algeria are long-standing rivals, and Western Sahara is one of their main points of friction.

causes.name: Mandate not renewed
causes.detail: The Security Council failed to renew MINURSO's mandate, which brought the mission to an end. Our sources do not give the vote details.

causes.name: Collapse of the truce in 2020
causes.detail: The ceasefire that gave MINURSO its role was declared over by the Polisario in 2020, which weakened the logic of the mission.

causes.name: Shifting great-power positions
causes.detail: US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty and Spain's later shift moved diplomatic weight towards Morocco. Background from general knowledge.

causes.name: Algeria's firmer posture
causes.detail: Algeria's troop deployment to Niger is its first abroad since 1973. It suggests Algiers is willing to project military power as UN monitoring recedes.

stakeholders.name: Morocco
stakeholders.role: Controls most of the territory and claims all of it
stakeholders.wants: International acceptance of its sovereignty, with autonomy as the framework
stakeholders.leverage: Control on the ground, diplomatic backing from some major powers
stakeholders.likelyMove: Welcome the end of the mission, push its autonomy framework, and avoid actions that invite blame for escalation

stakeholders.name: Polisario Front
stakeholders.role: Sahrawi independence movement, backed by Algeria
stakeholders.leverage: Armed capacity, refugee-camp base in Algeria, and the moral weight of the UN promise of a vote
stakeholders.likelyMove: Criticise the end of the mission and keep pressing its claim; the risk of renewed attacks is higher without monitors

stakeholders.name: Algeria
stakeholders.role: Main backer of the Polisario and Morocco's rival
stakeholders.wants: A self-determination outcome and a counterweight to Moroccan influence
stakeholders.leverage: Hosts the refugee camps and the Polisario, and has military capacity and a new willingness to deploy abroad
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep backing the Polisario diplomatically while managing a tense but still indirect rivalry with Morocco

stakeholders.name: UN Secretary-General and Secretariat
stakeholders.wants: A just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for self-determination
stakeholders.leverage: Good offices and reporting; no troops on the ground any more
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep supporting talks and warn of risks, as Guterres said on 1 November

stakeholders.name: UN Security Council members
stakeholders.role: Decided not to renew the mission
stakeholders.wants: Differs by member; our sources do not set out the positions
stakeholders.leverage: The mandate and the power to create a new mission
stakeholders.likelyMove: Stay divided; any new body would need fresh agreement, which looks unlikely soon

stakeholders.name: Spain
stakeholders.role: Former colonial power and the main European neighbour exposed to migration
stakeholders.wants: Stable relations with Morocco and Algeria and control of migration flows
stakeholders.leverage: Diplomatic ties, border cooperation and EU influence
stakeholders.likelyMove: Avoid taking sides, press for calm, and prepare for possible migration pressure

sectors.why: Without monitors, states and armed groups face fewer checks. Military planning and spending in the Maghreb may rise, though we have no figures.
A 35-year mission has ended without a settlement and without Council agreement to continue. That weakens the case for UN field presence in frozen conflicts.
Spain and the EU may need more capacity if tension raises departures towards Spain. This is an estimate.

sectors.sector: Morocco's phosphate, fishing and port activity in the territory
sectors.why: Fewer outside observers may help Morocco's operations politically, but renewed attacks would raise risk. Our sources do not cover these sectors, so confidence is low.

sectors.sector: Political risk insurance for Maghreb trade
sectors.why: Insurers may price more risk into routes and projects near the territory if security worsens. Speculative.
The mission was not a refugee agency, but its end may reduce UN visibility. The effect on aid is unclear.

dailyLife.effect: Many live in camps near Tindouf in Algeria, and others live in the territory. Fewer UN observers mean less outside visibility of their situation.

dailyLife.item: Travel and trade in the Maghreb
dailyLife.effect: There is no direct change reported yet. Any escalation would raise risks for travel and freight near the territory and for Morocco-Algeria relations.
Higher tension could bring more departures towards Spain. We have no figures, and this is a risk rather than an observed change.
No immediate effect on prices or services. The story matters because it shows how peace operations can end without a settlement.

scenarios.name: Quiet drift
scenarios.looksLike: The dispute stays frozen. Morocco and the Polisario trade statements. Few verified incidents. Diplomacy continues through the UN Secretary-General.
signposts: No major incident in the first three months
Guterres or an envoy keeps contacts open
Spain reports no unusual migration increase
scenarios.effectOnWorld: The region stays tense but stable. The UN's role shrinks quietly, and other disputes watch the precedent.

scenarios.name: Low-level clashes with competing accounts
scenarios.looksLike: Periodic attacks or shelling near the ceasefire line. Each side blames the other, and no neutral body can verify.
signposts: Polisario or Moroccan claims of attacks
Calls for a new monitoring arrangement
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Higher risk perception around the Maghreb. Spain and the EU watch migration. Pressure grows for some replacement observer arrangement.

scenarios.name: Diplomatic reset
scenarios.looksLike: A new push for talks, backed by major powers, perhaps with a lighter UN or regional monitoring arrangement.
signposts: A new UN envoy or high-level meeting
Council members discuss a new mechanism
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Lower risk, but a settlement would still be difficult because core positions have not moved.

scenarios.name: Wider escalation
scenarios.looksLike: Sustained fighting that draws Algeria and Morocco into direct confrontation or major cross-border incidents.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A serious regional crisis with risks for Spain, energy and trade routes, and the Sahel.

predictions.text: No new UN peacekeeping mission for Western Sahara will be authorised by the Security Council (about 90%).
Morocco and the Polisario will each publicly accuse the other of ceasefire-line attacks or violations, with no neutral verification (about 65%).
No direct, acknowledged military clash between Morocco and Algeria will occur (about 92%).
The UN Secretary-General will keep some political track for Western Sahara, such as an envoy or formal consultations (about 80%).
Spain will report a clear rise in arrivals on the Atlantic or southern route that officials link at least partly to regional tension (about 20%).

actions: Review exposure to projects or supply chains in or near Western Sahara and the Morocco-Algeria border area.
Add clear security and force-majeure terms for contracts touching the territory.
Monitor official travel advice for the Maghreb and Sahel.
Treat Maghreb political risk as slightly higher until it is clear whether the line stays quiet.
Watch for Council activity and for any statement from the Polisario ending its own commitments.
Do not assume escalation; no fighting has been reported in our sources.
Check government travel advice before visiting Morocco's southern provinces, Algeria's border areas or the Sahel.
Expect no immediate change in prices or services in Europe.
Explore a light monitoring or hotline arrangement between the parties to replace what MINURSO provided.
Keep the political process alive through the Secretary-General or a new envoy.
Prepare migration contingency planning with Morocco and other partners.
Coordinate on the wider Maghreb and Sahel picture, including Algeria's Niger deployment.

analogues.event: UN Emergency Force withdrawal from Sinai
analogues.whatFollowed: After Egypt asked UNEF to leave, war broke out within weeks. The cause was different, because the host asked the mission to go, but it shows the risk of a monitor vacuum.

analogues.event: UN Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea closes
analogues.whatFollowed: The mission ended after restrictions on its work. The border standoff stayed frozen for years rather than flaring immediately, until a later peace deal.
After the host government demanded the mission leave, fighting in the north resumed and the army retook territory such as Kidal. It shows that the end of a mission can reshape local power.

watch.title: Anniversary of Morocco's Green March
watch.why: Morocco marks the 1975 march each year. Expect strong statements on sovereignty, which may be tested by Polisario reactions.

watch.title: Anniversary of the 2020 ceasefire collapse
watch.why: A possible date for rhetoric or incidents from the Polisario.

watch.title: Security Council activity on Western Sahara
watch.why: Any move to create a replacement body or discuss the UN role would be an early sign of a diplomatic reset.

watch.title: Statements from the Secretary-General and any envoy
watch.why: Guterres said the UN stands ready to support a political solution. Concrete steps would show whether that role is real.

watch.title: Algeria's troop deployment to Niger and wider posture
watch.why: It signals a more assertive Algeria. Any link to the Western Sahara file would raise risk.

watch.title: Morocco-Algeria rhetoric and border incidents
watch.why: The strongest indicator of escalation risk.

watch.title: Spanish and EU migration figures
watch.why: The first hard evidence of any displacement effect.

confidence.claim: MINURSO ended on 1 November 2026 after 35 years, because the Security Council failed to renew its mandate
confidence.note: Reported by France 24; Al Jazeera and UN News report the end and wind-down. Vote details are not in our material.

confidence.claim: Morocco welcomed the decision; the Polisario opposed it
confidence.note: Morocco's welcome is stated by France 24. The Polisario's reaction is inferred from a truncated snippet.

confidence.claim: The UN warned of security risks and says it stands ready to support peace efforts
confidence.note: Al Jazeera headline and UN News report of Guterres's statement.
From general knowledge, not from the sources supplied; dates are as best recalled. Wikipedia is cited as general background.

confidence.claim: Algeria's troop deployment to Niger, its first abroad since 1973
confidence.note: Taken from the connected event; no source URL was supplied for it in the material, so it is not listed as a source.

confidence.claim: Possible knock-on effects for migration towards Spain
confidence.note: The event summary raises this as a risk. No data on arrivals is available; it is an estimate.
Author judgement, not a sourced forecast; to be graded as events resolve.

evidence.method: Drafted from three news and UN sources dated 1 November 2026, the matched wire headlines, and one connected event about Algeria's troop deployment to Niger. Historical background comes from general knowledge, with a Wikipedia page as a general reference. Our material includes few details on the Security Council vote, the Polisario's response and any security incidents, so the effects, scenarios and prediction probabilities are estimates.
